Let us flee the damages from laziness, let us avoid the poverty of virtues, and let us reject the shame of being weak in good things; let us become men and let our heart be strengthened, as it is written; for the Lord Jesus Christ gave us the examples of such virtue, saying that whoever does not take up their cross and follow him is not worthy of him; I think it is necessary to confess that following Christ is better than all cowardice; but to be overwhelmed by fear is to make one's own burden; just as a newborn child can barely walk and cannot follow the swift young men, so it is impossible for one who looks only to their own weakness to follow in the footsteps of Christ, who endured the cross, despising shame, and tasted the bitterness of death for us, although he was a passionless and immortal God, the Logos and the only-begotten Son of the Father, so that he might give us an example and a pattern for imitation, and on this very achievement Paul also was emboldened to courage

Become imitators of me, as I also of Christ. To whom then does the disciple of Christ, the soldier of Christ, hasten, who has been rightly chosen as our commander due to his virtue? He was so devoted to Christ that he considered it nothing to suffer everything, in order to become a genuine disciple of Christ. For he says, 'What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.' He was such a person in faith, and in his own character, he would astonish anyone who learned about him. For he made fasting his weapon in the battles of the body, and like a proven soldier, he subjected the laws of the flesh to the good things of his mind. He also overpowered the pleasure that tyrannized our limbs, as if he had taken one of his servants under his control, and subjected it to the will of the spirit. But in order to benefit us as well, he again exhorts us, saying that he had often been in fasts, and 'I beat my body and enslave it, lest after preaching to others, I myself become disqualified.' He was mindful, as it seems, of the cry of his own Master.

Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people thus will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; whoever does and teaches will be called great; the Lord preached and practiced, imposing fasting and abstinence on the flesh for virtue; his teachings go beyond self-control, guiding us to love; the Lord and Paul emphasize the importance of love, with Paul writing to the Corinthians about the superiority of love over other gifts

And if I distribute all my possessions and deliver my body to be burned, but have no love, I gain nothing. You see how, in the absence of love for God and for others, the most praiseworthy virtue appears unseemly and unattractive. But when love is present, it makes the glory of those who possess it most becoming. Would someone say that he praises love as a great and wonderful thing, but does not define its nature or show how one can attain it? You will not speak well, man. The sober disciple runs past nothing that is necessary. For not only did he teach that love for God and for others is precious, but he also shows how one can be a worker of love. He says again, 'Love is patient, love is kind, love does not envy, does not boast, is not puffed up, does not behave unseemly, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails.' You hear how, for those who want to ascend to the dignity of love and brotherly love, the matter is not difficult, but already prepared. You see that the path of approval from here is not hidden, but shines like the sun. Therefore, going through this path, and according to it, so to speak, coming in the chariot of the saints, we will arrive at the city above, whose craftsman and creator is God.

Turning away from the opposite and falling away from correct and straight opinion, then living a distorted life, we will end up in the depths of Hades, as the wise Proverb writer says. But I think it is necessary for us, being rational humans and made in the image of the Creator, to be guided by the laws of love and to imitate the Lord who says to learn from Him, that He is gentle and humble in heart, rather than sliding into the savagery of wild beasts and exchanging love for hatred. For wild beasts and irrational animals, although not governed by reason, somehow live together and have common habits. Cattle and sheep associate with their own kind, and even dogs, having been tamed by many and having a natural advantage, love each other like family members.
pass_b_english: We must flee from the damages that come from laziness and avoid the poverty of virtues, rejecting the shame of being weak in good things.
Let us become men and let our heart be strengthened, as it is written.
For the Lord Jesus Christ gave us the examples of such virtue, saying that whoever does not take up their cross and follow him is not worthy of him.
I think it is necessary to confess that following Christ is better than all cowardice, but to be overwhelmed by fear is to make one's own burden.
Just as a newborn child can barely walk and cannot follow the swift young men, so it is impossible for one who looks only to their own weakness to follow in the footsteps of Christ.

Christ, who endured the cross, despising shame, and tasted the bitterness of death for us, although he was a passionless and immortal God, the Logos and the only-begotten Son of the Father, gave us an example and a pattern for imitation.
And on this very achievement, Paul also was emboldened to courage.

The disciple of Christ, who is also a soldier of Christ, hastens to crown himself with the advantages of virtue, having been rightly chosen as our commander due to his virtue, and who also, as commander, was rightly appointed by vote.
He was so devoted to Christ that he considered it nothing to suffer everything in order to become a genuine disciple of Christ.
For he says, 'What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.' (Matthew 10:38)
He was such a person in faith, and in his own character, he would astonish anyone who learned about him.
He made fasting his weapon in the battles of the body, and like a proven soldier, he subjected the laws of the flesh to the good things of his mind.
He also overpowered the pleasure that tyrannized our limbs, as if he had taken one of his servants under his control, and subjected it to the will of the spirit.

But in order to benefit us as well, he again exhorts us, saying that he had often been in fasts, and 'I beat my body and enslave it, lest after preaching to others, I myself become disqualified.' (1 Corinthians 9:27)
He was mindful, as it seems, of the cry of his own Master.

The Lord teaches that whoever loosens one of the least commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; whoever practices and teaches these commandments will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
The Lord himself preached and practiced this, imposing fasting and abstinence on the flesh as a means to attain virtue.
The Lord's teachings go beyond self-control, guiding us towards the ultimate goal of love for one another.

This is emphasized by both the Lord and Paul, who writes to the Corinthians about the superiority of love over other gifts, stating that even the most extraordinary abilities are worthless without love.
The Lord's words, 'By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another,' highlight the importance of this virtue. (John 13:35)
The absence of love for God and for others makes even the most praiseworthy virtue appear unseemly and unattractive.
However, when love is present, it makes the glory of those who possess it most becoming.
If someone praises love as a great and wonderful thing, but does not define its nature or show how one can attain it, they will not speak well.
The sober disciple runs past nothing that is necessary, for they know that love is essential to true virtue.
The nature of love is described as patient, kind, and not envious or boastful; it does not behave unseemly, seek its own interests, or rejoice in iniquity.
Instead, it rejoices in the truth, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.
Love never fails, and it is the path to approval and the city above, whose craftsman and creator is God.
By following this path, we can arrive at the city above, coming in the chariot of the saints.

When we turn away from what is right and abandon our correct and straightforward judgment, we end up living a distorted life, which ultimately leads us to the depths of Hades, as the wise writer of Proverbs warns.

However, as rational human beings created in the image of our Creator, it is essential for us to be guided by the principles of love and to emulate the Lord, who teaches us to learn from Him and to cultivate gentleness and humility in our hearts.
In contrast to the savagery of wild beasts, which we should not imitate, even irrational animals and wild beasts are capable of living together and having common habits.
For instance, cattle and sheep associate with their own kind, and dogs, despite their natural instincts, can be tamed and learn to love each other like family members.
